description: United Anglo-Saxon kingdom (927–1707) emerging from Æthelstan's unification and consolidating through Plantagenet, Lancastrian, Yorkist, and Tudor dynasties; its constitutional development, Magna Carta (1215), Model Parliament (1295), common law, established institutional constraints on royal power that distinguished English governance from continental absolutism.

temporal.notes: Unified under Æthelstan; Norman conquest 1066, Plantagenets 1154

lifecycle_phases.description: Æthelstan (927) becomes the first king of all England after unifying the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms. Edgar 'the Peaceful' (959–975) codifies the relationship between Church and Crown. Æthelred II 'the Unready' faces massive Danish invasions and pays enormous Danegeld tributes. Cnut the Great conquers England (1016), ruling a North Sea Empire (England, Denmark, Norway). Edward the Confessor dies childless (1066), triggering a three-way succession crisis.

William the Conqueror defeats Harold at Hastings (1066), imposes Norman French as the language of government, and replaces the English aristocracy wholesale. The Domesday Book (1086) is an unprecedented survey of English landholding. Henry I builds an efficient bureaucracy. His death without a male heir triggers the Anarchy (1135–1154), civil war between Stephen and Matilda.

Henry II (1154–1189) rules an 'Angevin Empire' stretching from Scotland to the Pyrenees; his administrative reforms (Assize of Clarendon, common law courts) reshape English governance. His conflict with Archbishop Becket ends in Becket's murder (1170). Richard I goes on Crusade; John loses Normandy (1204) and seals Magna Carta under baronial pressure (1215). The minority of Henry III (1216–1272) sees ongoing baronial conflict (Second Barons' War, 1264–1267).

Edward I conquers Wales (1282–1283), wars repeatedly with Scotland (Wars of Independence 1296–1328), and expels Jews (1290). Edward III's Hundred Years' War victories (Crécy 1346, Poitiers 1356) are followed by the Black Death (1348) and peasant revolt (1381). Richard II's tyrannical rule ends in deposition (1399) by Henry Bolingbroke (Henry IV).

rise_factors.description: Henry II's legal reforms created the English common law system, royal courts, itinerant justices, jury trials, the most advanced legal order in medieval Europe; Magna Carta (1215) and the development of Parliament built institutions that constrained royal power while legitimizing it

England's island geography provided natural defense against continental invasion; after Hastings (1066), no foreign army successfully invaded England in the medieval period, allowing internal state-building without the constant military pressure faced by continental kingdoms

English wool exports were the foundation of the medieval European textile industry; the Florentine and Flemish cloth industries depended on English wool, giving English kings leverage over continental economies and credit networks

William the Conqueror's Domesday Book (1086), a comprehensive survey of landholding across England, enabled unprecedented fiscal extraction. No other medieval kingdom possessed comparable knowledge of its own resources; this administrative advantage persisted for generations.

Magna Carta (1215) established the principle that royal power was subject to law. While initially a feudal document, its reinterpretation over centuries created constitutional restraints on monarchy that distinguished England from continental absolutism.

English wool, particularly from Cistercian abbeys and large estates, was the highest-quality raw material for European cloth manufacturing. Wool export revenues funded English armies for the Hundred Years War and gave England exceptional leverage over Flemish cities dependent on English raw material.

The Welsh longbow adopted into English armies proved decisive at Crécy (1346) and Agincourt (1415): English archers could shoot 12 aimed arrows per minute, saturating opposing formations with fire before contact. This asymmetric advantage defeated much larger French armies.

decline_factors.description: The Angevin Empire required English kings to govern territories stretching from Scotland to the Pyrenees; the cost of defending these continental possessions, and the impossibility of ruling them from England, led to progressive loss of French territories

The Black Death (1348–1351) killed an estimated 30–45% of England's population; the Peasants' Revolt (1381) reflected the social disruption caused by labor shortages and collapsed agrarian relationships that the plague produced

The Hundred Years War (1337–1453) required unprecedented taxation: Edward III and Henry V financed campaigns through parliamentary consent, but persistent warfare created debt crises, baronial resentment, and ultimately the Wars of the Roses when military humiliation discredited the Lancastrian dynasty.

The Black Death killed 30–50% of England's population (1348–50). The resulting labor shortage empowered surviving peasants economically (higher wages), weakening serfdom, a structural economic transformation that produced both prosperity and social unrest.
